<explanation>
The AppFlowy Cloud project is a full‐stack, microservice-oriented application built in Rust. It provides secure user authentication, file storage, and real-time WebSocket communication for collaboration. The project is split into multiple components and crates that together form the complete system. Here’s how you can approach drawing the best and most accurate system design diagram for this project:

1. Main Components:
   - Frontend:
     • The “admin_frontend” directory is the dedicated admin interface. It contains assets, template files, and its own Dockerfile and Cargo configuration. This represents the user-facing web app for administration and dashboard purposes.
   - Backend Services:
     • Core Server Application: The “src” directory houses the main API endpoints (e.g., /api/access_request.rs, /api/user.rs, /api/ws.rs) that serve RESTful and WebSocket endpoints.
     • Microservices: Under the “services” directory, there are at least two key services:
       – appflowy-collaborate: Handles real-time communication, collaboration logic, and synchronization using Actix WebSocket and various sub-modules (collab, group, snapshot, etc.).
       – appflowy-worker: Handles background tasks such as email notifications, indexing, file imports, and data processing. 
   - Shared Libraries (libs):
     • The “libs” folder contains many sub-crates (e.g., authentication, client-api, database, mailer, access-control, etc.) that encapsulate domain logic and infrastructural functionality shared across different parts of the system.
   - Infrastructure & External Integrations:
     • Database: The project uses PostgreSQL. Migrations are maintained in the “migrations” directory.
     • Storage: Minio is referenced for file storage.
     • Caching & Message Queues: Redis is used, as hinted by debugging instructions and scripts.
     • Real-time and collaboration protocols: There are dedicated libraries for WebSocket interactions and real-time collaboration (e.g., client-websocket, collab-rt-entity).
     • External Tools: PgAdmin, Portainer, and a debug-friendly Nginx reverse proxy (from the nginx folder and Docker files) are also in play.

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   - The admin frontend interacts with the backend APIs to manage user sessions, authentication, and administration tasks.
   - The main server (in “src” and core libraries) communicates with the microservices via defined API endpoints and/or WS protocols.
   - The appflowy-collaborate service manages real-time communication with clients via WebSockets, using shared libraries for consistent data formats.
   - The appflowy-worker processes asynchronous jobs (indexing, email notifications, file processing) and interacts with the database, object storage, and external messaging queues.
   - The shared libraries are used across these components to enforce consistent business logic, authentication (libs/authentication), and error handling (libs/app-error).

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   - Modular Design and Microservice Architecture: Separation between frontend, backend APIs, and independent worker processes.
   - Domain-driven / layered design: Business logic is encapsulated in “biz” modules and shared crates.
   - Real-time Data Flow: Use of WebSocket components in both the API layer and dedicated real-time collaboration libraries.
   - Infrastructure-as-Code: Multiple Docker Compose files, Dockerfiles, and scripts ease deployment and testing.
   - Testing: A wide range of tests (unit tests in “tests”, integration tests in “services/*/tests”) ensures each module and service works as expected.

4. Technologies and Frameworks:
   - Rust as the main programming language.
   - Actix Web and Actix WebSocket for backend API and real-time communications.
   - sqlx for database connectivity and migration management.
   - Docker for containerizing services.
   - External integrations include PgAdmin for Postgres, Redis CLI, Minio for storage, and Portainer for container management.

5. Guidelines for Diagram Creation:
   a. Begin with a high-level box representing the AppFlowy Cloud ecosystem. Then create sub-boxes for:
      • Admin Frontend (Web UI)
      • API Gateway / Main Backend (from “src”)
      • Microservices:
         – Collaborate Service (appflowy-collaborate): Show its subcomponents such as WebSocket handling, collab management, group/plugin modules.
         – Worker Service (appflowy-worker): Indicate background processing like indexing, mailers, and file handling.
      • Shared Libraries: Central shared modules such as authentication, access-control, error handling, and client APIs. Connect these to both the API and services.
      • Databases and External Services:
         – PostgreSQL (with migration management)
         – Redis (for caching/queues)
         – Minio (for file storage)
         – Other tools: PgAdmin, Portainer, Nginx reverse proxy.
   b. Use directional arrows to illustrate communication channels:
      • Arrows from the admin frontend to the API.
      • Bi-directional arrows between the API and microservices (synchronization via WebSockets and API calls).
      • Arrows indicating asynchronous job flows from the API/services to the worker service.
      • Connect shared libraries as a common dependency module used by both the backend core and services.
   c. Use color coding or distinct shapes:
      • Rectangles for services and libraries.
      • Cylinders for databases.
      • Cloud symbols for external services.
      • Dashed lines for testing or monitoring flows.
   d. Label each component clearly with its name and role. For example, label “AppFlowy-Collaborate (Real-Time Service)” and annotate that it handles collaborative session communications.
   e. Consider layering the diagram:
      • Top layer: User interfaces and external access.
      • Middle layer: API backend and microservices.
      • Bottom layer: Persistence, messaging, and external integrations.

6. Extra Considerations:
   - Reflect the modularity by indicating the separation of concerns (API endpoints in “src/api”, business logic in “src/biz”, shared entities in “libs/shared-entity”).
   - Embed how configuration and deployment are handled by Docker Compose files and environment files (dev.env, deploy.env).
   - Incorporate testing and observability, as there are extensive test folders and telemetry modules.

By following these guidelines and tailoring your diagram with clear labels, directional flows, and differentiated colors/shapes for each type of component, you will capture the essential architectural elements and showcase a detailed view of AppFlowy Cloud’s design – from user interactions via the admin frontend to the granular inner workings of microservices and shared libraries, along with their integration with external systems.
</explanation>
